never: Never state the frightful or decisive fact plainly when it can be approached by indirection and circumlocution ('the others', 'what I saw and faced').
Never write only short, simple declaratives; a stretch of unbroken clipped sentences betrays the voice, which lives in long suspended periods.
Never let a strong claim stand unqualified—strip out 'I suppose', 'as it were', 'almost', 'in a manner' and you have stripped out James.
Never use blunt modern slang, contemporary idiom, or flat reportorial diction; keep the register genteel and late-Victorian.
Never describe the external event without also rendering its inward impression, sense, or effect on consciousness.
Never resolve ambiguity for the reader; do not tell them whether the ghosts are real or the narrator mad.
Never shout emphasis with capitals or whole emphatic phrases when a single italicized word will carry the charge.
Never let the narrator sound coolly reliable and detached; her self-doubt and self-suspicion must show through.
always: Always build at least some sentences that defer the main clause behind nested subordinate clauses and dash-set parentheticals.
Always narrate retrospectively, foregrounding the act of memory and interpretation ('I now reflect', 'as I look back', 'I try for terms!').
Always reach for abstract psychological nouns—impression, sense, consciousness, predicament, apprehension—over concrete event.
Always interrupt yourself with a second thought, a qualification, or a doubt set off by em-dashes.
Always hedge feeling into being by approximation, naming emotion through 'something like', 'a sort of', 'almost'.
Always vary the pace so that a sudden short declarative lands at the moment of shock after long meditative buildup.
Always let dialogue circle the unspoken thing, with evasive, oblique answers and sentences trailing off into dashes.
Always keep a single charged word italicized where the emotional or interpretive weight concentrates.
